# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review of Varga and Holm's Comment on the Halden Pilot

**Bottom line:** The first half of this comment is a valuable correction. The second half overreaches.

Three findings from the microdata are important and well documented:
- Seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals actually happened after the reduced schedule had started.
- Managers' output index exceeded the organisations' own records in 19 of 23 cases.
- Actual hours fell by 14%, not 20%.

Together these cut the per-hour gain roughly in half. But the paper's central conclusion is that the gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty." That claim is not supported. It contradicts the authors' own corrected estimate and the randomised evidence they themselves call the most reliable.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures reproduce:

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.800 | +18.9% ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Actual hours, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 | −14.1% ✓ |
| Actual hours, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 | −13.9% ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |

**One inconsistency in Section 3.** The stated sources of extra hours don't add up to the reported total:
- Baseline is 40.3 hours a week, or about 8.06 hours a day.
- Adding 0.7 hours to each of four days gives 4 × 8.76 = 35.0 hours.
- Adding 1.6 hours logged on the day off gives about 36.6 hours a week, not 34.6.

The figures fit if the 0.7 is *per week* rather than per day: 32.2 + 0.7 + 1.6 ≈ 34.6. Either the text or the total needs correcting.

## What the comment gets right

- **Attrition (§1)** is the most serious new finding. The working paper said the withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The comment shows that seven of nine withdrew after the schedule began, and that six of nine cited workload or output. That is a factual misstatement in the original report, not a judgement call.
- **The output measure (§2):** 19 of 23 managers exceeding the records is very unlikely by chance (sign test p ≈ 0.001). The authors' explanation, rounding toward success without bad faith, is fair.
- **The hours denominator (§3):** this measures directly what the original paper could only acknowledge as a limitation.
- **Revenue and sector claims (§4–5):** both are correct. They match the points I raised about the original paper.
- **The data note** is honest about the subsets. The problem is that the conclusion ignores it.

## Main problems

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the paper's own results

- **What the corrections show:** After correcting output and hours, the gain is +10.8%. The authors' corrections remove a bit over half of the original 23.4%, not all of it.
- **What closes the gap:** Getting from 10.8% to zero rests entirely on the novelty argument in §6. That argument is the paper's weakest section (point 4 below).
- **How the claim escalates:**
  - The abstract calls the residual "plausibly a novelty effect."
  - The same abstract then calls the gains "entirely an artifact."
  - The conclusion repeats "entirely" as a finding.
- **What the data note says:** The note itself says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion generalises beyond the pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" in general.

The evidence supports a weaker conclusion: the reported gain is overstated by about half, and whether the remainder lasts is unknown.

### 2. The comment uses the Varden trial selectively

The authors call Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature to date." But Varden's case-processing stratum came from the same trial and the same design:
- randomised;
- record-based output;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- nine months rather than six.

That stratum found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. It is the evidence that most directly tests the comment's thesis. Randomisation, administrative records and timesheets rule out all three of the artifacts the comment identifies, and the gain remained.

The comment doesn't mention this result. Citing one stratum of a trial as definitive while omitting the other is a serious problem for a paper whose argument is about selective evidence.

Varden's case-processing result has its own caveats, which I raised in my earlier review: cases closed may track demand rather than capacity, and only claimed overtime is captured. But those are reasons for caution, not grounds to treat the result as zero.

### 3. Attrition is never corrected, despite the abstract

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems. The first three are attrition, output and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours; attrition is argued but never quantified.

A rough bound shows attrition can't eliminate the gain. Suppose the nine withdrawn organisations had zero per-hour gain. The average across all 70 would then be about 61/70 × 10.8 ≈ 9.4%. To bring it to zero, the nine would need an average per-hour change of about −73%.

That calculation weights organisations equally and assumes the subset estimate applies to all 61, so it is illustrative only. But it shows attrition can trim the estimate, not remove it. The authors should report bounds like this rather than imply the effect is eliminated.

### 4. The novelty argument is weak

- **Two data points:** The decline is extrapolated linearly from two points (0.61 SD at month 3, 0.29 at month 6). Nothing supports a straight line rather than levelling off.
- **The extrapolation is wrong anyway:** A decline of 0.32 SD over three months reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten."
- **The wrong variable:** The argument extrapolates self-reported energy, not output. The pilot collected a *monthly* output index. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline across months 1–6, and that can be checked directly from the microdata. The authors had the data and didn't run the test.
- **Varden ran nine months:** Its case-processing gain was still clearly positive at month nine, past the point where the extrapolated novelty effect would have vanished.
- **Burden of proof cuts both ways:** "Six months is not long enough to distinguish novelty from a durable effect" is correct. But that means the question is open, not that the answer is zero.

### 5. The meetings section misdescribes the Varden analysis

The comment says the seven offices were "selected for analysis after the results were known." According to the Varden report:
- calendar data were collected in month six, at managers' request, during the trial;
- the seven offices were *all* the treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup;
- Varden labelled the analysis exploratory, said it "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test.

The underlying caution is fair. Seven offices is very few, r = 0.71 on n = 7 has a confidence interval that crosses zero, and there's no baseline meeting data. But the paper should criticise what Varden actually did.

The comment also ignores supporting evidence from its own dataset: 47 of 58 Halden managers independently mentioned cutting meetings. And the meetings hypothesis bears directly on §6. If gains come from removing low-value time, they need not fade as novelty wears off. Dismissing the hypothesis without engaging it removes the main alternative to the comment's own explanation.

### 6. Record-based output isn't automatically better

"Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types used. As an output measure, it is closer to an input measure. Billable hours divided by hours worked measures utilisation: more of the working week billed, less of it spent on unbillable tasks. That isn't productivity in the usual sense.

The comment treats the record-based index as the benchmark. The authors should report how many of the 23 used billable hours and test whether results change when those organisations are excluded.

## Smaller points

- **Retail subset:** the −11.2% figure comes from three organisations. That is too few to carry much weight.
- **Deflator:** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, since output prices differ by sector. Revenue also covers only 52 of 61 organisations. The direction of the point is still right.
- **"The only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work":** that claim needs a literature search behind it, or softer wording.
- **The counter result:** Varden's counter stratum had only 5 offices per arm, with a wide interval. Calling it "the most reliable finding in the literature" is strong for 10 clusters, although its direction is consistent with the Halden retail data.
- **Recommendations (§8):** these are sound. Intention-to-treat analysis of all enrolled organisations is especially important given §1.

## A conclusion the evidence supports

> Correcting for manager-reported output and scheduled hours roughly halves the Halden pilot's reported gain in output per hour, to about 11% in the subset where both corrections are possible. Non-random attrition, which the working paper misreported, likely biases the estimate upward further, though plausible bounds do not eliminate it. Whether the remaining gain persists is not established; the pilot's own monthly output data, and longer randomised follow-up such as Varden's 24-month study, can test this. Where output depends on staff presence, reduced hours reduce output.

## Taken together

Across the three documents, the picture is fairly consistent. The original Halden pilot overstated its results substantially. This comment correctly removes about half of the overstatement, then claims more than its evidence shows. The Varden trial remains the best evidence of the three. It suggests real but smaller per-hour gains in work not tied to presence, and real losses in work that is.

I can draft a reply letter to the editor, or a short synthesis of all three papers, if that would help.
